books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Uncle Sam’s Youngest Son, Citizen Know Nothing (Sarony & Co., lithograph, New York, 1854). Library of Congress, LCCN2003689281. Public domain.
stimulus.text: A lithograph published in New York in 1854, titled “Uncle Sam’s Youngest Son, Citizen Know Nothing.” It shows a young man in a wide-brimmed hat, wrapped in an American flag, with a plaque reading “CITIZEN” below him and an eagle above.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The Know-Nothing movement drew its strength most directly from which development of the 1840s and 1850s?

options.text: The discovery of gold in California.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the gold rush pulled people west; the Know-Nothings organized in Eastern cities where immigrants landed, not in the goldfields.

options.text: The annexation of Texas as a slave state.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Texas annexation sharpened the slavery debate, not the nativist one; Know-Nothing anger aimed at immigrants, not at Texas.

options.text: The building of the first transcontinental railroad.
options.misconception: Background from the books: no transcontinental railroad existed in the 1850s; the movement’s fuel was immigration, not railroads.

options.text: Large-scale Irish and German immigration to American cities.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the gold rush pulled people west; the Know-Nothings organized in Eastern cities where immigrants landed, not in the goldfields.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Texas annexation sharpened the slavery debate, not the nativist one; Know-Nothing anger aimed at immigrants, not at Texas.
rationales.C: Background from the books: no transcontinental railroad existed in the 1850s; the movement’s fuel was immigration, not railroads.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Irish and German newcomers crowded into Eastern cities in the 1840s and 1850s, and nativists organized to limit their rights and power.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who the cartoon is answering: immigrants, shown as a threat to the native-born citizen.
2. Background from the books: Irish and German arrivals surged in the 1840s and 1850s, mostly Catholic, mostly settling in cities.
3. Connect the surge to the movement: the Know-Nothings turned that arrival into a political cause.
Remember: a nativist movement names its moment; find the newcomers it fears.
